note: Original informational passages (origin 'llm', facts checked against standard references). Question sets cover RI.5.1 (detail/inference), RI.5.2 (main ideas), RI.5.4 (domain vocabulary), RI.5.5 (structure), RI.5.8 (reasons and evidence) and one short-text quotation item; some include L.5.4a context-clue items.

passages.title: Why the Caspian Is Called a Sea
passages.text: If you stand on the Boulevard in Baku and look east, you see water stretching all the way to the horizon. Most people call it the Caspian Sea, but geographers argue about that name. A true sea is connected to the world's oceans, while the Caspian is completely surrounded by land. That makes it the largest enclosed body of water on Earth, bigger than many countries. Five nations share its shoreline: Azerbaijan, Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Iran. So why do we call it a sea and not a lake? The main reason is its size, which is roughly the same as the whole of Japan. Another reason is its water, which is salty, although only about one third as salty as the ocean. Rivers such as the Volga pour fresh water into the northern end, so the north is much less salty than the south. The Caspian is also famous for an ancient fish called the sturgeon. Sturgeon have existed for millions of years and can grow longer than a car. Their eggs, known as caviar, were once so valuable that they were called black gold. Today the sturgeon is endangered, and fishing for it is strictly controlled. The sea has another surprising feature: its level rises and falls over the decades. In the 1930s the water dropped several metres, and old maps show harbours that are now far from the shore. Scientists believe that changes in rainfall and river flow cause these movements. Whether you call it a sea or a lake, the Caspian shapes life in Baku every day. Its winds cool the city in summer, its ports carry oil and grain, and its beaches fill with families every weekend.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do some geographers say the Caspian is not a true sea?
options: It is completely surrounded by land.
It is not salty at all.

distractor_rationale.D: it is about one third as salty as the ocean

questions.explanation: A true sea connects to the oceans; the Caspian is enclosed by land.
questions.rule: RI.5.1 — quote or find the stated detail.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Sturgeon are the biggest fish in the world.
The Caspian is an unusual body of water that is important to Baku.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph adds a reason the Caspian is unusual and important.
questions.rule: RI.5.2 — main idea supported by details.

questions.stem: In this passage, what does "enclosed" mean?
questions.explanation: The sentence before says it is completely surrounded by land.

questions.stem: How does the author organise the part about the sea's name?
options: By asking a question and then giving reasons that answer it.
By listing events in the order they happened.
By describing a problem and its solution.
questions.explanation: "So why do we call it a sea?" is followed by two reasons.

questions.stem: Which evidence does the author give to support the claim that the sea's level changes?
options: Old maps show harbours that are now far from the shore.
Sturgeon can grow longer than a car.
questions.explanation: The harbours on old maps are evidence of a lower water level.
questions.rule: RI.5.8 — reasons and evidence for a point.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that tells how salty the Caspian is compared with the ocean.
questions.rubric: Accept the sentence: Another reason is its water, which is salty, although only about one third as salty as the ocean. (Partial credit for quoting the phrase 'only about one third as salty as the ocean'.)
questions.explanation: That sentence compares the saltiness directly.

passages.title: How Bees Make Honey
passages.text: Honey begins as nectar, the sweet liquid that flowers produce to attract insects. A honeybee lands on a flower and sucks up the nectar with a tongue shaped like a straw. She does not swallow it into her ordinary stomach. Instead, she stores it in a special pouch called the honey stomach, which can hold almost as much as the bee weighs. A single bee may visit more than a hundred flowers before this pouch is full. Back at the hive, the forager passes the nectar to a house bee, mouth to mouth. The house bee holds it for a while and then passes it to another bee. Each time, the bees add substances from their bodies that break the nectar's sugars into simpler forms. This is why honey is easier to digest than raw nectar. The nectar is then placed into the six-sided wax cells of the honeycomb. At this stage it is still thin and watery, and it would soon spoil. To fix this, hundreds of bees fan their wings above the cells for hours. The moving air evaporates most of the water, until the honey becomes thick and sticky. Finally the bees seal each cell with a thin cap of wax, which keeps the honey clean and dry. A sealed cell of honey can last for many years without going bad. Making honey is enormous work for such small creatures. To produce one kilogram of honey, a hive's bees fly a distance equal to several times around the Earth. The honey is their winter food, stored when flowers are plentiful and eaten when the fields are bare. Beekeepers take only the extra honey and leave enough for the colony to survive until spring.

questions.stem: Where does a forager bee store nectar while flying back to the hive?
options: In wax cells on its legs

distractor_rationale.A: the text says she does not

questions.explanation: The passage names the special pouch: the honey stomach.

questions.stem: Which structure does the passage mainly use?
options: Steps in order, from nectar to sealed honey.
A comparison of bees and wasps.
A list of problems with beekeeping.
questions.explanation: The passage follows the process step by step.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states a main idea of the passage?
options: Honey is made through many steps that take a great deal of work.
questions.explanation: The steps and the flying distance both show the work involved.

questions.stem: "The moving air evaporates most of the water." What does "evaporates" mean?
options: turns liquid into vapour that leaves

distractor_rationale.D: the honey becomes thicker, not heavier

questions.explanation: Fanning removes water as vapour so the honey thickens.

questions.stem: Why do the bees fan their wings above the cells? Use the text's reasoning.
options: Because thin, watery nectar would spoil, so the water must be removed.
questions.explanation: The text says the watery nectar would soon spoil, so they evaporate the water.
questions.rule: RI.5.8 — reasons that support a point.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that explains what the honey is for.
questions.rubric: Accept: The honey is their winter food, stored when flowers are plentiful and eaten when the fields are bare. Must quote this sentence or its first clause.
questions.explanation: That sentence gives the purpose of honey for the colony.

passages.title: Where the Puddle Goes
passages.text: After a rain shower, a puddle appears on the playground. By the next afternoon it has vanished, yet nobody swept it away. Where did the water go? The answer is that it turned into a gas called water vapour and floated into the air. This change is called evaporation. It happens because water is made of tiny particles that are far too small to see. The particles are always moving, and the warmer they are, the faster they move. At the surface of the puddle, the fastest particles break free and drift away. Sunshine and wind speed this up, which is why puddles disappear quickly on a hot, breezy day. The water is not destroyed; it is simply spread out in the air as invisible vapour. You can prove the vapour is still there with a cold glass. Fill a glass with ice on a warm day and wait a few minutes. Drops of water soon appear on the outside of the glass. They did not leak through the glass. They came from vapour in the air, which cooled against the cold surface and turned back into liquid. This reverse change is called condensation. Evaporation and condensation are happening all around you, all the time. They dry your washing on the line, fog up the bathroom mirror, and form the clouds above the Caspian. When vapour high in the sky cools, it condenses into droplets that gather into clouds and eventually fall as rain. That rain makes new puddles, and the whole cycle begins again. Nothing is lost in this cycle. The same water particles that filled the playground puddle may once have been part of a cloud, a river, or even a dinosaur's drink.

questions.stem: What happened to the water in the puddle?
options: It turned into water vapour and went into the air.
It sank into the ground and disappeared forever.

distractor_rationale.A: the text says nobody swept it

questions.explanation: The passage says the water evaporated into the air.

questions.stem: What is "condensation" in this passage?
options: Water vapour turning back into liquid when it cools

distractor_rationale.D: rain is a result, not the process

questions.explanation: The text calls the reverse change condensation.

questions.stem: What evidence does the author use to show that vapour is really in the air?
options: Drops form on the outside of a cold glass.
questions.explanation: The cold-glass experiment shows vapour condensing.

questions.stem: The passage explains that heat makes evaporation faster. What kind of relationship is this?
questions.explanation: Warmth causes particles to move faster, which causes faster evaporation.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarises the passage?
options: Water moves between liquid and vapour in a cycle, and none of it is lost.
Playgrounds should be covered when it rains.
Clouds are made of ice only.

distractor_rationale.C: the text says they do not

questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the cycle idea directly.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that says the water in the puddle was not destroyed.
questions.rubric: Accept: The water is not destroyed; it is simply spread out in the air as invisible vapour. OR Nothing is lost in this cycle. Must quote one of them.
questions.explanation: Either sentence states that the water still exists.

passages.title: The Mud Volcanoes of Gobustan
passages.text: An hour's drive from Baku, the land looks like the surface of another planet. Small grey cones rise from the ground, and thick mud bubbles slowly at their tops. These are mud volcanoes, and Azerbaijan has more of them than any other country in the world. Scientists have counted more than three hundred, most of them near Gobustan and along the Caspian coast. A mud volcano is not like a fire volcano. It does not pour out red-hot lava. Instead, it pushes up a cold mixture of mud, water and gas from deep underground. The gas is mostly methane, the same gas that burns in a kitchen stove. Deep beneath the surface, layers of rock press on pockets of gas and water. The pressure builds up until the mixture forces its way through cracks in the ground. Most of the time the volcanoes only bubble and gurgle quietly. Every few years, however, one of them erupts with a roar. Mud shoots dozens of metres into the air, and sometimes the escaping gas catches fire and lights up the night sky. In 2001 a volcano near Baku sent flames hundreds of metres high, and people saw the glow from many kilometres away. Geologists study mud volcanoes because they reveal what lies far below our feet. The mud carries rock and minerals from several kilometres down, which would otherwise be impossible to reach. The volcanoes also show where oil and gas are hidden, since the same pressure that pushes up mud often comes from oil fields. Visitors are welcome to look, but signs warn them not to climb the cones. The mud may look calm, yet the ground beneath it is constantly shifting.

questions.stem: How is a mud volcano different from a fire volcano, according to the passage?
options: It pushes up cold mud, water and gas instead of hot lava.
It is found only in the sea.

distractor_rationale.D: they are on land near Gobustan

questions.explanation: The text says it does not pour out lava but a cold mixture.

questions.stem: What causes a mud volcano to erupt?
options: Pressure building up on gas and water deep underground
questions.explanation: Layers of rock press on gas and water until the mixture forces its way up.
questions.rule: RI.5.3 — cause and effect between ideas.

questions.stem: "Geologists study mud volcanoes because they reveal what lies far below our feet." What does "reveal" mean?
questions.explanation: The mud brings up rock from deep down, showing what is there.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that eruptions can be dramatic?
options: Azerbaijan has more than three hundred mud volcanoes.
In 2001 flames rose hundreds of metres and were seen from far away.
questions.explanation: The 2001 example shows how dramatic an eruption can be.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the last paragraph before the warning?
options: Mud volcanoes are dangerous to touch.
Scientists value mud volcanoes because they bring up material and clues from deep underground.
Oil is more important than gas.
questions.explanation: That paragraph explains why geologists study them.
questions.rule: RI.5.2 — main idea of a paragraph.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that tells what the gas in a mud volcano mostly is.
questions.rubric: Accept: The gas is mostly methane, the same gas that burns in a kitchen stove. Must quote this sentence or its first clause.
questions.explanation: That sentence names methane.

passages.title: Why a Steel Ship Floats
passages.text: Drop a steel spoon into the bath and it sinks at once. Yet a ship made of thousands of tonnes of steel floats across the Caspian every day. How can the same material sink in one shape and float in another? The secret is not the weight of the steel but the space it takes up. Scientists call this idea density, which means how much matter is packed into a certain amount of space. A spoon is solid steel, so it is far denser than water and sinks. A ship, however, is mostly hollow. Its steel walls surround an enormous space full of air, and air is extremely light. When you consider the whole ship, steel and air together, it is less dense than the water around it. That is why it floats. There is a second way to understand this. When a ship sits in the water, it pushes some water aside, or displaces it. The water pushes back with a force called buoyancy. If the weight of the displaced water equals the weight of the ship, the ship floats. A wide, deep hull displaces a great deal of water, so it can carry heavy cargo. This is why ships sit lower in the water when they are fully loaded. Engineers paint a line on the side of every large ship to show the safe limit. If the ship sinks below that line, it is carrying too much. You can test the idea yourself with a ball of modelling clay. Roll it into a ball and it sinks. Flatten the same clay into a bowl shape and it floats, because the bowl takes up more space with the same amount of clay. The clay has not changed, but its density has.

questions.stem: Why does a steel spoon sink?
options: It is solid steel and denser than water.

distractor_rationale.D: the ship is hollow, not the spoon

questions.explanation: The passage says a spoon is solid steel and far denser than water.

questions.stem: What does "density" mean in this passage?
options: How much matter is packed into a certain space
questions.explanation: The passage defines density directly.

questions.stem: How does the author organise the explanation?
options: By comparing a spoon and a ship, then giving two explanations and an experiment.
By telling the story of one ship.
questions.explanation: Comparison → density → buoyancy → clay experiment.

questions.stem: How does the clay experiment support the author's point?
options: It shows the same material can sink or float depending on its shape and density.
It shows clay is heavier than steel.
It shows ships should be made of clay.
questions.explanation: The clay has not changed, only its density.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A ship floats because, taken as a whole, it is less dense than the water it displaces.
Ships should be painted with a line.
questions.explanation: Both explanations (density and buoyancy) support this single idea.
questions.rule: RI.5.2 — main idea supported by details.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that explains what the line painted on a ship's side shows.
questions.rubric: Accept: Engineers paint a line on the side of every large ship to show the safe limit. Must quote this sentence.
questions.explanation: That sentence explains the purpose of the line.

passages.title: Silk and Stone: The Caravanserais of Sheki
passages.text: Long before trains and lorries, goods travelled across Asia on the backs of camels. Merchants moved in groups called caravans, which could include hundreds of animals and people. Their routes, known together as the Silk Road, linked China with Europe. Silk was the most famous cargo, but caravans also carried spices, glass, paper, carpets and ideas. One important stop lay in the green foothills of the Caucasus: the town of Sheki. Sheki had something the merchants wanted very much. Its farmers raised silkworms on mulberry leaves and spun the thread into fine cloth. Traders arrived to buy it and stayed for days, so the town needed somewhere safe for them to sleep. The answer was the caravanserai, a kind of hotel built for caravans. From the outside it looked like a fortress, with thick stone walls and a single gate that closed at night. Inside was a wide courtyard where the camels rested and drank. Around the courtyard ran two floors of small rooms, one for each merchant, with storage for the goods below. Sheki's two great caravanserais were built in the 1700s and 1800s, and they still stand today. Visitors can walk through the same arched gateway that once welcomed tired traders. A caravanserai was more than a place to sleep. Merchants from many lands ate together, compared prices, and swapped stories. News of new ideas travelled along the Silk Road as surely as the silk itself. When steamships and trains arrived, the camel caravans slowly died out. Yet the caravanserais of Sheki remain, and they remind us that trade has always carried more than goods.

questions.stem: What was a caravanserai?
options: A kind of hotel built for caravans
questions.explanation: The passage defines it directly.

questions.stem: Why did Sheki need caravanserais?
options: Because traders came to buy silk and stayed for days.
Because the town had no farmers.
questions.explanation: Traders stayed for days, so the town needed safe lodging.
questions.rule: RI.5.3 — cause and effect in history.

questions.stem: "Merchants moved in groups called caravans." What is a "merchant"?
options: a person who buys and sells goods
questions.explanation: Merchants trade goods.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the last paragraph?
options: Caravanserais were places where ideas and news were exchanged, not just goods.
questions.explanation: The paragraph ends: trade has always carried more than goods.

questions.stem: How is the description of the building organised?
options: From the outside to the inside.
From the newest part to the oldest.

distractor_rationale.D: walls and gate first, then courtyard and rooms

questions.explanation: Walls and gate first, then courtyard, then rooms.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that lists goods other than silk that caravans carried.
questions.rubric: Accept: Silk was the most famous cargo, but caravans also carried spices, glass, paper, carpets and ideas. Must quote this sentence.
questions.explanation: That sentence lists the other cargo.

passages.title: Why Your Brain Needs Sleep
passages.text: Every night you close your eyes and stop noticing the world for eight or nine hours. It looks as if nothing is happening, but your brain is busier than you might think. Scientists who study sleep have discovered that the sleeping brain does several important jobs. The first job is sorting memories. During the day you learn hundreds of things: a new word, a maths method, the way to a friend's house. While you sleep, the brain replays these experiences and decides which ones to keep. Students who sleep well after studying remember more the next day than students who stay up late. The second job is cleaning. Brain cells produce waste as they work, just as a busy kitchen produces rubbish. During deep sleep, fluid flows through the brain and washes this waste away. Without enough sleep, the waste builds up, and thinking becomes slow and foggy. The third job is growing. The body releases a growth hormone mostly during sleep, which is one reason children need more sleep than adults. Health experts recommend nine to eleven hours a night for children aged six to thirteen. Many children get far less, often because of screens. The light from a phone or tablet tells the brain that it is still daytime, so the brain delays the signal to feel sleepy. Doctors suggest putting screens away an hour before bed and keeping the bedroom dark and cool. Sleep is not wasted time. It is when the day's learning becomes permanent, when the brain tidies itself, and when the body grows. A good night's sleep may be the most useful homework of all.

questions.stem: What are the three jobs of the sleeping brain described in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage names each job in order.
questions.rule: RI.5.2 — two or more main ideas.

questions.stem: How much sleep do health experts recommend for children aged six to thirteen?
questions.explanation: The passage states nine to eleven hours.

questions.stem: What evidence supports the claim that sleep helps memory?
options: Students who sleep well after studying remember more than those who stay up late.
questions.explanation: The comparison of students is evidence for the memory claim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do screens make it harder to fall asleep?
options: Their light tells the brain it is still daytime.
questions.explanation: The light delays the sleepy signal.

questions.stem: "Thinking becomes slow and foggy." What does "foggy" mean here?
questions.explanation: Foggy thinking is unclear, like seeing through fog.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that compares brain waste to something in a kitchen.
questions.rubric: Accept: Brain cells produce waste as they work, just as a busy kitchen produces rubbish. Must quote this sentence.
questions.explanation: That sentence contains the kitchen comparison.

passages.title: Which Way Is Down?
passages.text: Drop a pencil and it falls to the floor. Throw a ball upwards and it always comes back. Something invisible is pulling everything towards the ground, and we call that pull gravity. Gravity is a force between any two objects that have mass. Your body pulls on the Earth, and the Earth pulls on your body. The Earth wins because it is enormously more massive than you are. This is why you feel pulled down, while the Earth barely notices you at all. Here is a question that puzzled people for a long time. If the Earth is round, why don't people on the other side fall off? The answer is that gravity does not pull towards some floor in space. It pulls towards the centre of the Earth. For a person in Baku, down means towards the centre. For a person in Australia, down also means towards the centre, even though the two people are standing in opposite directions. Everybody on the planet is held on by the same pull towards the same point. Gravity also explains why rain falls, why rivers flow downhill, and why the Moon stays close to the Earth instead of drifting away. Astronauts on the space station look as if they have escaped gravity, but they have not. Gravity there is still almost as strong as on the ground. The astronauts float because they and their station are falling around the Earth together, very fast. You can feel a small version of this when a lift starts to go down and your stomach seems to rise. Scientists measure the pull of gravity carefully. On Earth, a falling object speeds up by almost ten metres per second every second. On the Moon, which has much less mass, the pull is only about one sixth as strong, which is why astronauts there could jump so high.

questions.stem: Towards where does gravity pull objects on Earth?
options: Towards the centre of the Earth
questions.explanation: The passage states this directly.

questions.stem: The author asks why people on the other side of the Earth do not fall off. What does this question do in the passage?
options: It introduces a common misunderstanding and then explains the correct idea.
It changes the subject to the Moon.
It shows the author is unsure.
questions.explanation: The question sets up the explanation about the centre of the Earth.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, do astronauts float on the space station?
options: Because there is no gravity in space.
Because they and the station are falling around the Earth together.
Because the station is on the Moon.

distractor_rationale.A: the text says gravity is almost as strong there

questions.explanation: The passage explains that they are falling together, not that gravity is gone.

questions.stem: "The Earth wins because it is enormously more massive than you are." What does "massive" mean here?
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter; the Earth has far more.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the whole passage?
options: Gravity pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth and explains many everyday events.
Astronauts can jump high on the Moon.
questions.explanation: The passage keeps returning to the centre-of-Earth idea and its effects.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that tells how strong the Moon's gravity is compared with Earth's.
questions.rubric: Accept the sentence beginning: On the Moon, which has much less mass, the pull is only about one sixth as strong… Must include 'one sixth'.
questions.explanation: That sentence gives the comparison.
